periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem Aloud and First Responses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond — I (p.126): paired discussion, listing childhood memories to share.
Reflect and Respond — II (p.126): class discussion on mother–child emotional bonds.
Reflect and Respond — III (p.126): matching six poem words to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Pre-reading warm-up: students work in pairs on Reflect and Respond — I, listing childhood memories and briefly sharing with the class. The teacher invites two or three pairs to share aloud.
Whole-class discussion on Reflect and Respond — II: how a mother's presence shapes a child's emotions and memories. The teacher steers towards the poem's themes of loss and sensory belonging.

The teacher reads the poem aloud with expression, students following in their textbooks (p.126); then individual students are invited to read one stanza each for a second unhurried pass. Stage directions, line breaks, and the refrain are observed closely.

Students work individually on Reflect and Respond — III (p.126), matching the six poem words to their meanings; pairs compare answers and the teacher confirms with brief word-in-context notes from the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's refrain 'I cannot remember my mother' paradoxically makes her presence pervasive rather than absent — draw students' attention to this tension during the read-aloud. The tone is tender and quietly melancholic, so model a slow, reflective reading pace rather than a dramatic one. Students who find the vocabulary matching easy may be prompted to use each word in a sentence drawn from their own experience.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for vocabulary matching display

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding — I (p.127–128): stanza-by-stanza fill-in on setting and key details.
Check Your Understanding — II (p.128): complete the senses table for all three stanzas.

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding — III (p.128–129): eight questions on alliteration, onomatopoeia, tone, title, refrain, and symbolism — complete independently.

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly invites students to recall the poem's three stanzas and their sensory anchors (auditory, olfactory, visual) without reopening books, as a quick oral retrieval. This frames the close reading that follows.

Students work individually on Check Your Understanding — I (p.127–128), completing the stanza-by-stanza fill-in blanks for setting, season, and key details; the teacher circulates and asks probing questions — 'What word tells us the setting is outdoor?' — before whole-class verification.

Teacher introduces the senses table task from Check Your Understanding — II (p.128) with the example row on the board; students complete the table for all three stanzas, then pairs cross-check; the class constructs a full table together on the board, with students reading the exact lines from the poem that carry each sensory reference.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently conflate the olfactory stanza (shiuli scent + temple fragrance) with the auditory stanza (the lullaby tune) — reinforce that each stanza is anchored to a distinct sense, though the stanzas overlap emotionally. The poem uses imagery extensively: the hovering tune, the floating scent, and the gaze spread across the sky are all extended visual or sensory images that carry the mother's presence without direct description. Homework flagged above covers alliteration, onomatopoeia, tone, title impact, refrain, and symbolism — alert students to look closely at the poem text and use the poem_appreciation_summary angle when thinking about the sky as symbol.
materials: Textbook, p.126–129 (poem + Check Your Understanding apparatus)

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection on Extracts and Sensory Vocabulary in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection — II (p.131): four extended-answer questions on refrain impact, nature's role, and mother–child relationship.
Vocabulary in Context — I (p.131): classify sensory words into Visual, Auditory, Olfactory, Tactile categories.

time_bands.activity: Teacher returns to the poem's refrain — 'I cannot remember my mother' — read aloud once, and asks: what is the emotional paradox? Brief whole-class responses settle the class into analytical mode.

Students work individually on Critical Reflection — II (p.131): all four extended-answer questions on the emotional impact of the refrain, the connection between the mother and shiuli flowers and the humming tune, nature's role, and inferences about the mother–child bond. After individual writing, the teacher facilitates a discussion, cold-calling on two or three students per question and building a shared response on the board.

Teacher introduces Vocabulary in Context — I (p.131): students work in pairs to sort the sensory word box into Visual, Auditory, Olfactory, and Tactile columns. The teacher connects this directly to the poem's sensory architecture — 'Which column would the poem's shiuli scent fall under?' — before pairs share their classifications with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The Critical Reflection questions demand inferential and evaluative responses: students should be steered away from simple plot summary and towards the symbolic weight of shiuli flowers (gentle, devotional spirit) and the sky (eternal extension of the mother's gaze) as developed in the poem. A common difficulty is distinguishing 'nature as backdrop' from 'nature as active symbol' — prompt students to say what each natural image does, not just what it describes. Vocabulary classification works best when students read each word aloud and mime or describe the sensation it evokes before categorising it.
materials: Textbook, p.126–132 (poem + Critical Reflection + Vocabulary in Context apparatus)
Blackboard for response notes and sensory-word classification grid

periods.activity_title: Listening to Childhood Memories and Sharing Personal Recollections

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond — I (p.133): match six statements to four speakers; two statements are not needed.
Speaking Activity — I (p.133): paired oral presentation on a memorable object, song, or place using structured prompts.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets context for the listening task: four speakers will share childhood memories in different registers and settings; students should listen for the distinctive detail that anchors each speaker's memory, not just its subject.

Teacher reads aloud the four transcript extracts (p.266) at a measured pace; students listen and complete the matching task from Listen and Respond — I (p.133), matching statements 1–6 to speakers, noting that two statements are unused. After a second read of any extract where answers are uncertain, the class verifies answers together.

Students prepare for Speaking Activity — I (p.133) individually for two or three minutes, noting their memorable object, song, or place and the five prompts. Pairs then take turns presenting, with each partner speaking for an unhurried stretch; the teacher circulates and prompts for sensory detail and emotional reflection where students remain at the surface level.

periods.teacher_notes: In the listening task, students often conflate Statement 3 (school-days recollection) with Statement 5 (grandparents and funny tales), which both involve Speaker iii — the key difference is the grandpa's comic-strip lap-sitting detail that is specific to Speaker iii and the class discussion thread that is absent. The speaking task benefits from a brief teacher-modelled example using one of the poem's sensory moments ('Tagore's lullaby tune in the midst of play') as a scaffold before students speak about their own memories. Encourage students to use sensory language they encountered in the Vocabulary in Context work.
materials: Transcript text (p.266 of transcript booklet) for teacher to read aloud
Blackboard for matching-task display during verification

periods.activity_title: Diary Entry on Sensory Memory and Exploring India's Unique Flowers

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task — I (p.133): guided diary entry describing a sensory school trip, including format, emotions, and reflection.
Learning Beyond the Text — I (p.133): gather and share information on unique flowers of India, their scent, appearance, and cultural significance.

homework.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text — II (p.133): collect poems or songs on family and memory in English and your own language; read Thomas Hood's poem and note similarities with Tagore's.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the diary entry format on the board using the guidance in Writing Task — I (p.133): day, date, time; first person throughout; sensory-detail structure across the five senses; emotional register and closing reflection. A brief class discussion names two or three scenic places students might write about.

Students draft their diary entry independently following the guided format. The teacher circulates, prompts students to expand thin sensory descriptions ('What did you hear? What did the air smell like?'), and gives formative oral feedback on one or two sentences per student where possible.

A quick pair-share: each student reads one sentence with strong sensory detail from their draft to their partner and receives one word of encouragement and one suggestion. Students may revise that sentence immediately.

Teacher introduces Beyond the Text — I (p.133) using the shiuli flower information in the textbook as the anchor. Students brainstorm two or three other unique Indian flowers they know (e.g. Neelakurinji, lotus, night-flowering jasmine) and discuss their sensory and cultural associations in small groups before sharing with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The diary entry should be self-contained — drafted and peer-reviewed within this sitting rather than carried over. A common weakness is a list of sensory details without emotional anchoring; prompt students to link each detail to a feeling, as Tagore links the shiuli scent to devotion and the mother's gentle spirit. The Beyond the Text discussion on Indian flowers works well when students connect a flower's sensory character (scent, colour, blooming time) to a human emotion or cultural practice, mirroring the poem's symbolic method.
materials: Textbook, p.133–136 (Writing Task + Beyond the Text apparatus)

items.source_lo: Student analyses sensory imagery, poetic devices, and the emotional architecture of a lyric poem using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tagore's refrain, sensory memories of lullaby, shiuli scent, and the mother's gaze across the sky.
items.item_stem:
In the first stanza of the poem, the speaker says a tune seems to hover over his playthings. Which of the following best describes what the hovering tune represents?
A. The speaker's enjoyment of playing alone.
B. A faint, involuntary sensory trace of the mother's presence.
C. A deliberate effort to call the mother to mind.
D. The sound of other children playing nearby.

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker's enjoyment of playing alone.

options.label: B
options.text: A faint, involuntary sensory trace of the mother's presence.

options.label: C
options.text: A deliberate effort to call the mother to mind.

options.label: D
options.text: The sound of other children playing nearby.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates the playful setting with the emotional content of the stanza; misses the intruding quality of the tune.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Mistakes involuntary sensory memory for deliberate recollection; the poem stresses the tune 'seems to hover', not that the speaker summons it.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reads the tune as external sound rather than an internalised memory surfacing during play.

items.source_lo: Student analyses sensory imagery, poetic devices, and the emotional architecture of a lyric poem using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Tagore's refrain, sensory memories of lullaby, shiuli scent, and the mother's gaze across the sky.
items.item_stem:
Read the third stanza on p.126, beginning “I cannot remember my mother.”

1. What does the image of the mother's gaze spreading across the sky suggest about the speaker's perception of his mother?
2. Tagore uses the sky as a symbol in this stanza. Explain what the sky symbolises and how the visual image extends the poem's emotional meaning.
3. The poem ends on a visual impression rather than an auditory or olfactory one. Evaluate the effect of this choice on the poem's overall tone.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the third stanza on p.126, beginning “I cannot remember my mother.”

expected_elements: Mother's gaze is infinite, protective, and not bounded by physical absence.
Sky symbolises eternity and the omnipresence of the mother's love.
Visual image extends emotional meaning: the mother watches from everywhere, always.
Ending on visual impression creates a sense of expansive, unending stillness.
Tone shifts from melancholic longing to quiet, almost consoling, belonging.

items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and distinguishes between speakers' distinct memories using a listening-and-responding task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four speakers' childhood memories — grandfather's voice, beach trips, grandparents' comic-strip tales, carefree outdoor play.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the four speakers describing their childhood memories (transcript p.266). State whether each of the following statements is true or false, and write one phrase from the corresponding speaker's account that supports your answer.
(1) Speaker (i)'s grandfather used a question about bravery to lift the speaker's spirits.
(2) Speaker (ii) remembers playing indoors as the defining joy of childhood.
(3) Speaker (iii) always remembered the comic-strip stories accurately when retelling them in the kitchen.
(4) Speaker (iv) found the beach exactly as they had left it when they returned after several years.

options.text: Speaker (i)'s grandfather used a question about bravery to lift the speaker's spirits.
Speaker (ii) remembers playing indoors as the defining joy of childhood.
Speaker (iii) always remembered the comic-strip stories accurately when retelling them in the kitchen.
Speaker (iv) found the beach exactly as they had left it when they returned after several years.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) True — grandfather asked 'who is the bravest one?' and the speaker shouted 'Me', which still uplifts them. (2) False — Speaker (ii) describes outdoor activities: chasing butterflies, making paper boats, playing on sandy beaches. (3) False — Speaker (iii) forgot the real narratives and ended up babbling. (4) False — the once serene beach was now crowded when Speaker (iv) returned after a decade.

items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and distinguishes between speakers' distinct memories using a listening-and-responding task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four speakers' childhood memories — grandfather's voice, beach trips, grandparents' comic-strip tales, carefree outdoor play.
items.item_stem: Having listened to all four speakers, choose ONE speaker whose childhood memory involves a loss or change — not just a happy recollection. In two or three sentences, explain what changed and why this memory carries both joy and a sense of distance.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Speaker (iv) describes the beach as a cherished childhood memory, but when the family returned after a decade, the once serene beach was crowded and the carefree closeness within the family had been replaced by a sense of distance. The memory carries joy because the childhood beach days were genuinely happy, but also loss because those conditions cannot be recovered.

items.item_stem: Think of a sound — a voice, a song, or a recurring noise — that immediately takes you back to a specific childhood moment. Describe that sound and the memory it unlocks in two or three spoken sentences, making sure to name at least one other sense you associate with that memory.

expected_elements: Names a specific sound linked to a childhood moment.
Identifies at least one additional sense associated with the memory.
Describes the emotional quality of the memory briefly but clearly.

items.item_stem: Tagore argues, through his poem, that we can carry the presence of a person we have lost through sensory memory alone — a tune, a scent, a quality of light. Do you agree that sensory memory is a reliable or meaningful way to hold on to someone we cannot directly remember? Present your view with at least one reason and one example from either the poem or your own experience.

expected_elements: States a clear position — agree, disagree, or partially agree.
Provides at least one reasoned argument supporting the position.
References a specific sensory detail from the poem or personal experience.
Engages with the idea of 'reliability' or 'meaning' rather than just describing memory.
Maintains a coherent spoken argument without reading from notes.

items.item_stem: Write a short notice (60–80 words) for your school notice-board announcing a poetry-reading event where students will share poems or songs that evoke childhood memories. Include the event's name, date, venue, who it is open to, and one sentence inviting participation.

expected_elements: Uses notice format: title, date, venue, and issuing body clearly stated.
Stays within the 60–80 word limit.
Includes an inviting sentence that names childhood memory or sensory experience.
Formal, impersonal register appropriate to a school notice-board.

items.item_stem: Write a letter to the editor of a literary magazine (120–150 words) arguing that poetry which relies on sensory memory — smell, sound, sight — connects with readers more deeply than poetry that describes emotions directly. Use at least one specific example from a poem you have read to support your argument.

expected_elements: Uses formal letter-to-editor format with salutation and sign-off.
States a clear central argument about sensory versus direct emotional poetry.
Cites at least one specific image or line from a poem as evidence.
Develops reasoning — explains why sensory detail creates deeper connection.
Maintains a formal, persuasive register throughout within the word limit.

items.source_lo: Student classifies and applies sensory domain vocabulary in context using a poem-themed vocabulary task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Sensory word classification — visual, auditory, olfactory, tactile — drawn from the poem's imagery world.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below describe moments from the world of Tagore's poem — autumn mornings, temple courtyards, a child's bedroom. Rewrite each sentence by replacing the word in brackets with a more precise sensory word. Then name the sense (visual, auditory, olfactory, or tactile) the new word appeals to.

1. The (nice) fragrance of shiuli flowers drifted through the courtyard at dawn.
2. From the bedroom window, a (far) blue sky stretched beyond the rooftops.
3. A (soft) lullaby seemed to float across the silent room.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sample answers: 1. 'sweet' or 'delicate' — olfactory. 2. 'vast' or 'distant' — visual. 3. 'hushed' or 'gentle' — auditory. Accept any precise sensory adjective that improves on the bracketed word and correctly identifies the associated sense.

items.source_lo: Student extends understanding of cultural and natural symbolism through interdisciplinary research using a poem's imagery as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Unique flowers of India — their sensory qualities, cultural significance, and symbolic resonance across Indian traditions.
items.item_stem: The shiuli (Parijat) flower is described in the textbook as blooming at night, releasing a sweet fragrance, and being revered in Indian ceremonial life. Write a short paragraph (60–80 words) explaining what sensory qualities of a flower — any flower found in India — could make it a powerful symbol in a poem about memory. Name the flower, describe at least two of its sensory qualities, and explain the symbolic connection.

expected_elements: Names a specific Indian flower and at least two sensory qualities.
Explains clearly why those qualities connect to memory or emotion.
Uses precise sensory vocabulary (not vague words like 'nice' or 'good').
Shows awareness that symbols carry cultural or emotional meaning beyond appearance.
Paragraph is coherent and within the word limit.

items.source_lo: Student extends understanding of cultural and natural symbolism through interdisciplinary research using a poem's imagery as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Unique flowers of India — their sensory qualities, cultural significance, and symbolic resonance across Indian traditions.
items.item_stem: Design a short research project (outline only — no more than eight bullet points) in which you investigate two flowers native to different regions of India. Your outline should state: the two flowers chosen; the region or state each comes from; the key sensory detail you will research (scent, colour, bloom season, or texture); the cultural practice or legend you will explore; and how you plan to present your findings to the class (poster, spoken presentation, illustrated notes, or another format).

expected_elements: Names two distinct Indian flowers from different regions.
Identifies the region or state associated with each flower.
Specifies at least one sensory quality to be researched per flower.
Includes a cultural practice, legend, or ceremonial use for at least one flower.
States a clear presentation format and gives a reason for that choice.
